title: Hillel and Shammai, Akhnai and "These and Those"
bigQuestion: When wise people disagree about a rule, how did the rabbis of the Talmud decide, and what did they do with the side that lost?

story.title: The Voice That Was Overruled
story.kicker: A heavenly voice takes one side in a debate, and the rabbis politely say that it does not get a vote.
paragraphs: Picture a study hall in the Land of Israel around the year 100 CE. The floor is stone. Men sit in rows on low benches. At the front, a teacher named Rabbi Eliezer is arguing about an oven. It is a strange oven, built from pieces with sand between them. Can it become ritually impure, or not? Rabbi Eliezer says it cannot. Every other rabbi in the room says it can.

The Talmud, in the tractate Bava Metzia on page 59b, tells what happened next. Rabbi Eliezer gave every argument he had. The others did not accept them. So he said: if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The story says the tree tore itself out of the ground and moved. The rabbis answered that a tree proves nothing. He called on a stream of water, and it ran backward. He called on the walls of the study hall, and they began to lean. Still the rabbis said no.

Then Rabbi Eliezer called on heaven itself. The story says a voice came from the sky and asked why they argued with him, since the law always followed him. At that moment Rabbi Joshua stood up. He quoted a line from the Torah, from Deuteronomy chapter 30: the Torah "is not in heaven." A later teacher, Rabbi Jeremiah, explained what he meant. The Torah was already given at Mount Sinai. Now people decide its meaning, and they decide by majority.

That is only half the story. The Talmud goes on to tell what the majority did after they won, and how their treatment of Rabbi Eliezer caused great pain. The whole passage sits inside a discussion about hurting people with words. So the story is about two things at once. It is about who has the authority to decide. It is also about how to treat the person who loses.

In this chapter you will meet the two great Houses, Hillel and Shammai, who argued for years until a voice said that both spoke truth. You will read the Oven of Akhnai in paraphrase, first half and second half. You will see how the Mishnah keeps the opinions that lost. And you will ask what it means to argue for the sake of heaven.
story.think: Rabbi Joshua would not let a miracle settle an argument. What do you think a good argument should be settled by?

lessons.title: The Houses of Hillel and Shammai
lessons.mainIdea: Hillel and Shammai were two teachers around 30 BCE, and the schools named for them disagreed on hundreds of rules.
reading: Hillel and Shammai were two teachers who lived in Jerusalem around 30 BCE, in the time of King Herod. The Mishnah names them as the last of the *zugot*, the pairs of leaders who came before the rabbis. Hillel is remembered in the Talmud as patient and gentle. Shammai is remembered as strict and quick. Each gathered students, and each group kept teaching after its founder died.

The students formed two schools. The Talmud calls them *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai*, the House of Hillel and the House of Shammai. The word beit means house. The two Houses argued about hundreds of questions. How should the Hanukkah lamps be lit? What may a person carry on Shabbat? Which blessing comes first at a meal? Most of the time, Beit Shammai took the stricter reading and Beit Hillel the more lenient one. Not always.

The Mishnah records both sides of these debates. In most cases it does not say who won. That is important. The Mishnah, edited around the year 200 CE, was written long after both Houses were gone. By then Jewish practice followed Beit Hillel almost everywhere. Yet the editors kept Beit Shammai's words on the page. The next lesson tells the story the Talmud gives for why.

words.d: the pairs of leaders named in Pirkei Avot who came before the rabbis; Hillel and Shammai were the last pair
the House of Hillel; the school of students who followed Hillel's way of reading the law
the House of Shammai; the school of students who followed Shammai's stricter readings

look.title: Teachers in Order
rows: Hillel and Shammai teach in Jerusalem (c.)
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua at Yavneh (c.)
look.cite: Dates as historians commonly give them; see the outline of rabbinic generations in any introduction to the Talmud
look.prompt: About how many years passed between Hillel's teaching and the closing of the Talmud that records it?

check.q: What does the word beit mean in Beit Hillel?
check.why: Beit means house. Beit Hillel is the House of Hillel, the school of his students.

check.q: In most debates between the two Houses, which took the stricter view?
check.why: Beit Shammai usually took the stricter reading and Beit Hillel the more lenient one, though not in every case.

check.q: How does the Mishnah usually record a debate between the Houses?
choices: It gives only the winning view
It gives only Beit Shammai's view
It gives both views, often without saying who won
check.why: The Mishnah keeps both sides on the page and often does not say which one practice follows.

lessons.title: "These and Those"
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud in Eruvin 13b says a heavenly voice called both Houses' words "the words of the living God" but ruled with Beit Hillel.
reading: The tractate *Eruvin* is about the boundaries of Shabbat, where a person may walk and carry. On page 13b it pauses for a story. The Gemara says that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argued for three years. Each side said: the law follows us. Then a *bat kol*, a voice from heaven, spoke. The Gemara reports its words this way: these and those are the words of the living God, and the law follows Beit Hillel.

Readers have found this puzzling for centuries. If both are the words of the living God, how can one side be wrong? The Gemara does not treat the two as one right and one wrong. It treats them as two true ways to read the Torah. Yet a community needs one practice. People must know which lamp to light and which blessing to say first. So the voice picked one for daily life without calling the other false.

Different Jewish readers explain this in different ways. Some traditional commentators say each House saw a real side of the truth. Some modern academic readers say the story reflects a time when Beit Hillel had already won, and the story explains why. Rabbinic tradition holds both ideas together: the argument is kept, and one ruling is followed. This is the pattern for the whole Talmud.

words.d: a tractate of the Talmud about the boundaries of Shabbat; its name means mixings or joinings
a voice from heaven; literally daughter of a voice; a sound the Talmud says was heard in some stories

look.title: The Voice in Eruvin
look.text: The Gemara tells that the two Houses argued for three years, each saying the law followed them. Then a heavenly voice went out and declared that these and those are the words of the living God, and that the law follows the House of Hillel.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b; paraphrased from the Aramaic and from Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud (1896–1903), tract Erubin
look.prompt: The voice says two things. Which part is about truth, and which part is about what people should do?

check.q: What is a bat kol?
check.why: Bat kol means daughter of a voice. In the Talmud it is a voice from heaven heard in certain stories.

check.q: According to Eruvin 13b, what did the voice say about the words of the two Houses?
choices: Both are the words of the living God
Only Beit Hillel's words are true
Only Beit Shammai's words are true
check.why: The Gemara reports that the voice said these and those are the words of the living God, and then ruled with Beit Hillel for practice.

check.q: Which tractate holds the story of the three-year argument?
check.why: The story is on Eruvin 13b. Bava Metzia holds the Oven of Akhnai; Avot is the book of sayings.

lessons.title: Why the Law Follows Hillel
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara says Beit Hillel earned the ruling by being humble and teaching the other side's view first.
reading: The Gemara in Eruvin 13b asks a fair question. If both Houses spoke the words of the living God, why did the voice pick Beit Hillel? The answer it gives is not about being smarter. It says the students of Hillel were kind and humble. They taught their own opinions and the opinions of Beit Shammai. And when they taught, they put Beit Shammai's words before their own.

Think about what that means in a classroom. Before you say why you are right, you say what the other side thinks, in their words, fairly. You even say it first. The Gemara treats this habit as a reason to trust a school's rulings. A teacher who has really listened to the other side is more likely to get the law right. And a community can follow such a teacher without feeling that one side was crushed.

The Gemara adds a lesson it draws from the story: whoever makes themselves low, the Holy One raises up. Rabbinic tradition reads the Hillel story as a lesson in *anavah*, humility. Historians add another layer. The Mishnah was edited by Judah the Prince, who traced his family line to Hillel. Both readings can be true of the same text. One is about character; the other is about who was holding the pen.

words.d: humility; the habit of not putting yourself above others, which the Talmud praises in Beit Hillel
the rabbi who edited the Mishnah around 200 CE; rabbinic tradition traces his family to Hillel

look.title: Say the Other Side First
look.text: Two students disagree about whether a class should have a phone box at the door. Student A says: Here is what B thinks, and here is the best reason for it. Now here is what I think. Student B says: I am right, and anyone can see it. The class must choose whose plan to try.
look.prompt: Using the Gemara's reason for following Beit Hillel, which student's plan would the rabbis be more likely to trust, and why?

check.q: What habit of Beit Hillel does the Gemara give as a reason the law follows them?
choices: They taught Beit Shammai's view before their own
They never disagreed with each other
check.why: Eruvin 13b says Beit Hillel taught both views and put Beit Shammai's words first, out of humility.

check.q: What does anavah mean?
check.why: Anavah is humility. The Gemara reads the Hillel story as a lesson in it.

check.q: What extra point do historians add about Beit Hillel winning?
choices: The editor of the Mishnah traced his family to Hillel
The voice was heard in Babylonia
check.why: Judah the Prince, who edited the Mishnah, is said to descend from Hillel, which may help explain the record.

lessons.title: The Oven and the Miracles
lessons.mainIdea: In Bava Metzia 59b, Rabbi Eliezer calls on a tree, a stream and walls to prove his ruling, and the sages refuse each one.
reading: The story begins in the Mishnah, in the tractate Kelim, which deals with vessels. An oven was built in pieces, with sand packed between them. Rabbi Eliezer said that such an oven could not become ritually impure, because it was not really one object. The other sages said it could. The Mishnah calls it the oven of *Akhnai*. The Gemara says the name means snake, because the arguments wound around it like a snake.

The Gemara in *Bava Metzia* 59b tells what happened. Rabbi Eliezer brought every proof he could think of. The sages did not accept them. So he said: if the law is with me, let this carob tree prove it. The tree pulled itself up and moved a long way. The sages answered that no proof comes from a carob tree. He said: let the stream prove it. The water ran backward. They said no proof comes from a stream.

Then he said: let the walls of the study hall prove it. The walls began to fall in. Rabbi Joshua scolded the walls. He said that when scholars argue about the law, walls have no business joining in. The Gemara adds a gentle detail. Out of respect for Rabbi Joshua the walls did not fall, and out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer they did not stand straight again. They stayed leaning.

Notice what the sages are doing. They never say the miracles did not happen. They say the miracles are not the kind of proof that counts. A rule of the Torah is decided by reasons and by the vote of the scholars. Rabbi Eliezer, a tanna of the generation after the Temple's fall in 70 CE, was one of the greatest scholars alive. That is what makes the story hard, and the next lesson shows the turn.

words.d: the name of the oven in the story; the Gemara connects it to a word for snake because the arguments coiled around it
the middle gate; a tractate about finding, buying, borrowing and wages, which holds the Akhnai story on page 59b
Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, a tanna around 100 CE, student of Yochanan ben Zakkai, who ruled that the oven was pure

look.title: Three Proofs Refused
look.text: A carob tree moves. A stream runs uphill. The walls of the room lean in. After each one, the sages say the same thing: this is not proof. Rabbi Joshua even tells the walls to stay out of the argument.
look.prompt: Why might the rabbis have decided that a wonder, even a real one, should not settle a question about the law?

check.q: What was Rabbi Eliezer's ruling about the oven?
check.why: Rabbi Eliezer said the oven, built in pieces with sand between, could not become ritually impure. The sages disagreed.

check.q: On which page of the Talmud is the Akhnai story told?
check.why: The Gemara tells the story in Bava Metzia 59b. Eruvin 13b holds the story of the Houses.

check.q: What did the sages say each time a miracle happened?
choices: That it proved Rabbi Eliezer right
That it was not proof in a legal argument
check.why: The sages did not deny the wonders. They said a tree, a stream and walls are not proof about the law.

lessons.title: "It Is Not in Heaven"
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Joshua answers the heavenly voice with Deuteronomy 30:12, and Rabbi Jeremiah explains that the law is decided by majority.
reading: Rabbi Eliezer had one proof left. He said: if the law is with me, let heaven prove it. The Gemara says a *bat kol* went out and said: why do you argue with Rabbi Eliezer, when the law follows him in every place? This was the moment. A voice from heaven had taken a side. The whole room heard it.

Rabbi Joshua stood on his feet and quoted the Torah. The verse is Deuteronomy 30:12, and it says the commandment "is not in heaven." In Deuteronomy the verse means that the Torah is not far away or too hard to reach. Rabbi Joshua reads it in a new way. The Torah has already been given. It is on earth now, in the hands of people who study it.

The Gemara asks what Rabbi Joshua meant, and it lets a later teacher explain. Rabbi Jeremiah, an amora who taught in the Land of Israel in the fourth century, says: the Torah was already given at Mount Sinai, so we pay no attention to a heavenly voice. He points to another verse, Exodus 23:2, which the rabbis read as: follow the *majority*. Once the Torah was given, the rule is decided by the vote of the scholars.

This is one of the most quoted moments in the Talmud. Readers have used it to say that the law lives in human hands and human argument. Others add that this freedom has limits: the majority must reason from the text, not invent. Notice too that Rabbi Joshua does not call the voice a lie. He says it is not the way the law is decided. The Gemara has one more scene, and it changes everything.

words.d: Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, a tanna around 100 CE, who answered the heavenly voice with a verse
the larger part of a group; the rabbis read Exodus 23:2 as a rule to decide the law by the vote of the majority
an amora of the fourth century in the Land of Israel who explains Rabbi Joshua's words in the Gemara

look.title: The Verse Rabbi Joshua Quoted
look.text: It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say: 'Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, and make us to hear it, that we may do it?'
look.cite: Deuteronomy 30:12, JPS Tanakh (1917); quoted by Rabbi Joshua in Bava Metzia 59b
look.prompt: In Deuteronomy the verse says the Torah is close and possible to do. How does Rabbi Joshua use the same words to make a different point?

check.q: Which verse did Rabbi Joshua quote to answer the heavenly voice?
check.why: Rabbi Joshua quoted Deuteronomy 30:12, "It is not in heaven." Leviticus 19:18 is "love your neighbor."

check.q: Who explains in the Gemara what Rabbi Joshua meant?
check.why: Rabbi Jeremiah, a later amora, explains that since the Torah was given at Sinai, a heavenly voice is not followed.

check.q: Which verse do the rabbis read as the rule to follow the majority?
check.why: Rabbi Jeremiah points to Exodus 23:2, which the rabbis read as a command to incline after the majority.

lessons.title: Elijah's Report
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Nathan meets the prophet Elijah, who says that God laughed and said, "My children have defeated me."
reading: The Gemara adds a short scene. Rabbi Nathan, a tanna of the second century, met the prophet *Elijah*. In rabbinic stories Elijah is a figure who did not die and who appears to certain rabbis to tell them things. Rabbi Nathan asked him: what did the Holy One do at that hour, when Rabbi Joshua overruled the voice?

Elijah answered that God laughed and said: my children have defeated me, my children have defeated me. In the story the response is not anger. It is something like a parent's delight when a child wins an argument fairly. Rabbinic tradition reads this as approval. The rabbis were supposed to take the Torah into their own hands and reason with it.

Different readers stress different things here. Many traditional readers see the laugh as proof that human courts have real authority. Some academic readers point out that the story was told by rabbis and gives authority to rabbis, so it should be read as their own view of themselves. Both agree on what the text does: it makes the majority's decision stand, and it makes heaven agree.

Stop and notice the shape of the *sugya* so far. A Mishnah states a dispute. The Gemara brings proofs, and each is rejected. A voice gives an answer, and a verse answers the voice. A later amora explains the verse. A story confirms the result. This is a full argument, with every move in place. And then the Gemara asks what happened next.

words.d: a prophet of the Hebrew Bible; in rabbinic stories he appears to some rabbis and reports what happens in heaven
one unit of Talmudic argument on a topic, with its question, proofs, objections and answers

look.title: "My Children Have Defeated Me"
look.text: Rabbi Nathan met Elijah and asked what the Holy One did in that hour. Elijah answered that God laughed and said: my children have defeated me, my children have defeated me.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b; paraphrased from the Aramaic (compare Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903, tract Baba Metzia)
look.prompt: The word defeated usually sounds like a loss. Why do you think the story shows God laughing instead of angry?

check.q: Who reports what God said when the voice was overruled?
check.why: Rabbi Nathan meets the prophet Elijah, who reports that God laughed and said, "My children have defeated me."

check.q: What is a sugya?
choices: one unit of Talmudic argument on a topic
a book of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: A sugya is a single passage of Talmudic argument with its question, proofs, objections and answers.

check.q: How does rabbinic tradition usually read the laugh in the story?
choices: As a sign the story is false
As a warning to Rabbi Nathan
As approval of the rabbis deciding by majority
check.why: Traditional readers take the laugh as heaven's delight that the rabbis reasoned for themselves.

lessons.title: The Ban and the Wave
lessons.mainIdea: The second half of the story shows the majority hurting Rabbi Eliezer, and it sits inside a discussion of wronging people with words.
reading: The Gemara does not end with the laugh. It says that on that day the sages gathered everything Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and burned it. Then they voted to place him under a *ban*, a kind of separation from the community. They asked: who will go and tell him? Rabbi Akiva, his own student, said he would, so that no one less careful would break the news and destroy the world.

Rabbi Akiva dressed in black and sat at a distance. Rabbi Eliezer asked why this day was different. Rabbi Akiva said gently that it seemed his friends were keeping away from him. Rabbi Eliezer understood. He tore his clothes and wept. The Gemara says that at that hour a third of the olives, wheat and barley in the world were struck. It is telling the reader that his pain was not small.

Rabban Gamliel, the head of the court, was on a ship. A great wave rose against him. He said: I know this is because of Rabbi Eliezer. He prayed that he had not acted for his own honor but to stop disputes from spreading, and the sea grew calm. Later, his sister Imma Shalom, who was Rabbi Eliezer's wife, tried to keep her husband from a certain prayer. One day she failed. The Gemara says Rabban Gamliel died. Told gently, the point is this: the majority won, and it still caused harm.

Why is this story in Bava Metzia, a tractate about money? Because the Mishnah before it, Bava Metzia 4:10, is about *ona'at devarim*, wronging with words. The Gemara says that all the gates of heaven may be locked except the gate through which a wounded person's cry enters. The Akhnai story is placed there as an example. Rabbi Eliezer was wronged with words. Authority and mercy are argued on the same page.

words.d: in the Talmud, a formal separation from the community for a time; the sages placed one on Rabbi Eliezer
wronging with words; hurting someone by what you say, which the Mishnah forbids in Bava Metzia 4:10
Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh, head of the court around 100 CE, who oversaw the ban on Rabbi Eliezer

look.title: One Story, Two Halves
look.text: First half: the majority overrules a heavenly voice, and heaven laughs. Second half: the majority burns Rabbi Eliezer's rulings, bans him, and his weeping brings harm to the world and to the head of the court. The Gemara tells both halves in one breath, inside a discussion about hurting people with words.
look.prompt: Why do you think the editors of the Talmud kept the second half instead of ending the story at the laugh?

check.q: Which Mishnah does the Akhnai story sit inside?
choices: Bava Metzia 4:10, on wronging with words
Avot 1:1, on the chain of tradition
check.why: The Gemara tells the story while discussing ona'at devarim, wronging with words, from Bava Metzia 4:10.

check.q: Who went to tell Rabbi Eliezer about the ban?
check.why: Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Eliezer's own student, went dressed in black so the news would be given gently.

check.q: What does the Gemara say about the gates of heaven in this passage?
choices: The gate for a wounded person's cry is never locked
check.why: The Gemara says all gates may be locked except the gate of wronging, the cry of a person hurt by words.

lessons.title: Rabbi Joshua and the Emperor's Daughter
lessons.mainIdea: In Ta'anit 7a, Rabbi Joshua answers an insult about his looks with a lesson about plain jars and good wine.
reading: Rabbi Joshua ben Hananiah, the same teacher who answered the heavenly voice, appears in many stories with Romans. The tractate *Ta'anit*, which is about fast days, tells one on page 7a. The emperor's daughter said to him: such beautiful wisdom in such an ugly vessel. She was mocking his face. He did not get angry. He asked a question instead.

He asked her what her father kept his wine in. She said: in plain clay jars. He said: everyone keeps wine in clay jars. A great emperor should keep his in gold and silver. So she had the wine moved into gold and silver vessels, and it turned sour. When she asked him why, he said: wisdom is the same. It keeps best in a plain vessel.

The Gemara adds a small twist. She asked whether there were not handsome people who were also wise. He said yes, but they would be wiser if they were plain. The story is *aggadah*, a story rather than a law. It shows the rabbis' picture of Rabbi Joshua: quick, calm and able to turn an insult into a lesson without returning it. That is the same skill he used against the voice from heaven.

words.d: a tractate of the Talmud about fast days and prayers for rain; it holds many stories of the rabbis
the stories, sayings and ethics in the Talmud, as opposed to halakhah, the law

look.title: Wine in a Gold Jar
look.text: Someone tells you that your idea is good but you do not look like a person who could have thought of it. You could answer with an insult of your own. Rabbi Joshua answered with a question about wine jars, and let the other person find the answer.
look.prompt: What does the story suggest about the best way to answer someone who is being rude?

check.q: What did the emperor's daughter say to Rabbi Joshua?
choices: That his wisdom was in an ugly vessel
That he should become a Roman
That the wine had turned sour
That the Torah is not in heaven
check.why: She mocked his looks, saying such beautiful wisdom sat in an ugly vessel. Ta'anit 7a tells the story.

check.q: What happened when the wine was put in gold and silver jars?
check.why: The wine soured in the fine vessels, and Rabbi Joshua used that to say wisdom keeps best in a plain one.

check.q: What kind of text is this story?
check.why: The story is aggadah: a tale that teaches character, not a legal ruling.

lessons.title: Keeping the Minority Voice
lessons.mainIdea: Mishnah Eduyot 1:4–6 explains why the opinions that lost are still written down.
reading: A small tractate of the Mishnah called *Eduyot*, meaning testimonies, asks a question most law books never ask. Why record the words of a single sage against the majority, when the law follows the majority? The Mishnah gives two answers in its first chapter, in mishnayot 1:4 through 1:6.

The first answer, in Eduyot 1:4, is about the Houses. Why keep Shammai's and Hillel's words when they were not accepted? To teach future generations that a person should not stand stubbornly on their own words, since even these great teachers did not have every word accepted. The second answer, in 1:5, is about courts. A later court may see the *minority* view and rely on it, because it was recorded. If it were erased, no one could ever use it.

This is the opposite of how many systems work. In many places the losing side is forgotten. The Mishnah keeps it. Rabbi Judah, in Eduyot 1:6, adds a third reason: so that if someone later says, I have a tradition like this, you can answer, you heard it from that individual, not from the majority. Keeping the minority view lets you know exactly what is and is not the rule.

Historians note that this habit is one reason the Talmud looks the way it does: pages of disagreement rather than a list of answers. For readers of the Akhnai story, it adds something. Rabbi Eliezer lost the vote. His opinion is still on the page, with his name. Being overruled is not the same as being erased.

words.d: testimonies; a tractate of the Mishnah that collects rulings and explains why minority views are kept
the smaller part of a group; in the Talmud, the opinion that did not win the vote but is still recorded

look.title: Why Write Down the Losing Side?
look.text: The Mishnah asks why the words of an individual are recorded alongside the majority, when the law follows the majority. It answers: so that a later court may see the individual's words and rely on them. It adds that the words of the Houses are kept to teach that one should not insist on one's own opinion.
look.cite: Mishnah Eduyot 1:4–5; paraphrased from the Hebrew (compare Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud, 1896–1903, which includes tract Eduyoth)
look.prompt: Name one thing that could go wrong if a law book erased every opinion that lost a vote.

check.q: What does the name Eduyot mean?
check.why: Eduyot means testimonies. It is a tractate that collects rulings and explains why minority views are kept.

check.q: According to Eduyot 1:5, why keep a single sage's view against the majority?
choices: Because the majority is usually wrong
Because the sage paid for it
Because a later court may rely on it
Because the voice from heaven said so
check.why: The Mishnah says a later court may see the recorded minority view and rely on it.

check.q: What lesson does Eduyot 1:4 draw from keeping the rejected words of Hillel and Shammai?
choices: That the Houses were wrong about everything
That only Hillel should be studied
That a person should not stand stubbornly on their own words
check.why: Eduyot 1:4 says even these great teachers had words that were not accepted, so no one should insist on their own opinion.

lessons.title: For the Sake of Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Pirkei Avot 5:17 says an argument for the sake of heaven lasts, and it names Hillel and Shammai as the example.
reading: *Pirkei Avot*, the Chapters of the Fathers, is a tractate of the Mishnah made entirely of sayings. In chapter 5, mishnah 17, it sorts arguments into two kinds. An argument that is for the sake of heaven will endure. An argument that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure. Then it gives one example of each.

The example of an argument for the sake of heaven is Hillel and Shammai. The example of the other kind is Korah and his group, who in the book of Numbers rebelled against Moses. Readers have asked what "endure" means here. Many say it means the argument keeps giving fruit: both sides are studied, both are remembered, and people keep learning from it. The Houses' debates are still studied today. Korah's rebellion ended and taught nothing.

What makes an argument for the sake of heaven? Commentators such as Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, who wrote on the Mishnah in the fifteenth century, say it is one in which both sides want the truth, not victory. Each side is willing to be shown wrong. Both sides respect the other. That fits Beit Hillel teaching Beit Shammai's view first. It also gives a way to think about the Akhnai story: the argument was for the sake of heaven, and yet the way it ended still hurt.

This mishnah is often used in Jewish schools and adult study today, across Orthodox, Conservative and Reform communities, as a rule for how to disagree. In a public school it can be read the same way any wisdom text is read: as one tradition's answer to a question everyone faces. When you argue, are you trying to win, or trying to find out what is true?

words.d: Chapters of the Fathers; a tractate of the Mishnah made of sayings about how to live and study
a figure in the book of Numbers who led a rebellion against Moses; Avot uses him as the example of a bad argument
Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura, an Italian rabbi of the fifteenth century whose commentary on the Mishnah is printed with it

look.title: Two Kinds of Argument
look.text: The mishnah says that every dispute that is for the sake of heaven will in the end endure, and one that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure. It gives the dispute of Hillel and Shammai as the first kind and the dispute of Korah and all his company as the second.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 5:17; paraphrased (compare Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, 1877)
look.prompt: Why does the mishnah name the two people in the good argument, but only Korah and his group in the bad one, and not Moses?

check.q: Which example does Avot 5:17 give of an argument for the sake of heaven?
check.why: Avot 5:17 names Hillel and Shammai as the argument for the sake of heaven, and Korah as the other kind.

check.q: What does the mishnah say happens to an argument for the sake of heaven?
choices: It is settled by a voice
It is decided by the emperor
check.why: The mishnah says such an argument will in the end endure; readers take this to mean it keeps teaching.

check.q: Who was Bartenura?
choices: A tanna who argued with Hillel
A fifteenth-century commentator on the Mishnah
check.why: Rabbi Ovadiah of Bartenura wrote a commentary on the Mishnah in the fifteenth century that is printed with the text.

lessons.title: How Readers Read Akhnai Today
lessons.mainIdea: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers all use the Akhnai story, and each draws a different lesson from it.
reading: The Oven of Akhnai is one of the most discussed passages in the Talmud. Different Jewish readers use it to say different things. Many *Orthodox* readers stress that the majority won because it followed the rules of the Torah itself, including the verse about the majority. For them the story shows that the law is decided by trained scholars using the text, not by miracles and not by whatever a person feels.

Many *Conservative* readers stress the same story as proof that the law grows through human decision. If the rabbis could overrule a heavenly voice, then later courts can also make changes, as long as they reason from the sources. Many *Reform* readers go further and read the story as a charter for human freedom and conscience in interpreting tradition. These are ways of reading one text; the text does not settle which is right.

Academic readers, in universities including those in Chicago, often ask a different set of questions. Who told this story and when? The heroes are rabbis, and the story gives authority to rabbis. Its second half, they note, was likely edited into place by the Talmud's redactors to fit the theme of wronging with words. Some also compare the version in the Jerusalem Talmud, which is shorter.

None of these readings has to be the only one. The Talmud itself kept the argument, the voice, the laugh, the ban and the wave together. A reader in a public school can do the same: describe what the text says, describe how each group reads it, and then think for yourself. That is what this unit means by argument. The next chapter turns to the other thread, mercy.

words.d: a branch of Judaism that holds the Oral Torah and its law as binding as tradition has passed them down
a branch of Judaism that holds Jewish law as binding but changeable through the decisions of its rabbis
a branch of Judaism that treats Jewish law as guidance and stresses individual conscience and ethics

look.title: Same Story, Four Readers
look.text: Reader A: the majority won because it used the Torah's own rule. Reader B: the rabbis showed that later courts may change the law with good reasons. Reader C: the story is a charter for conscience. Reader D: rabbis told a story that gives rabbis authority; look at who was holding the pen.
look.prompt: Pick two of the readers. What do they agree the text says, and where does their reading of it part ways?

check.q: Which reading treats the Akhnai story as showing that later courts may change the law with good reasons?
check.why: Many Conservative readers use the story to show that the law grows through human decision from the sources.

check.q: What kind of question do academic readers usually ask about the story?
choices: Which branch of Judaism is right
Who told the story and when, and how it was edited
check.why: Academic readers ask about authors, editors and dates, for example whether the second half was joined to the first later.

check.q: What does the chapter say about which reading is correct?
choices: The text itself does not settle which is right
check.why: The chapter describes how each group reads the story and leaves the judgment to the reader, as a study course does.

review.q: Where is the story of the heavenly voice saying "these and those are the words of the living God"?
review.why: Eruvin 13b tells of the three-year argument between the Houses and the voice that ruled with Beit Hillel.

review.q: Why does the Gemara say the law follows Beit Hillel?
choices: They had a bigger study hall
They were humble and taught Beit Shammai's view first
review.why: Eruvin 13b credits Beit Hillel's humility, including teaching the other side's words before their own.

review.q: What did Rabbi Joshua do when the heavenly voice supported Rabbi Eliezer?
choices: He quoted Deuteronomy 30:12, "It is not in heaven"
review.why: Rabbi Joshua answered the voice with the verse, and Rabbi Jeremiah explained that the law is decided by majority.

review.q: What did Elijah say God did when the rabbis overruled the voice?
choices: Laughed and said, "My children have defeated me"
review.why: Rabbi Nathan reports Elijah's words: God laughed and said his children had defeated him.

review.q: What theme of the Mishnah is the Akhnai story placed under?
review.why: The story appears in the Gemara on Bava Metzia 4:10, the Mishnah about ona'at devarim, wronging with words.

review.q: What does Mishnah Eduyot say about opinions that lost the vote?
choices: They are recorded so a later court can rely on them
They belong only to Beit Shammai
review.why: Eduyot 1:5 says minority views are kept because a later court may see them and rely on them.

review.q: In Avot 5:17, what is the example of an argument that is not for the sake of heaven?
choices: Rabbi Joshua and the emperor's daughter
review.why: Avot 5:17 names Korah and his company as the argument that does not endure, and Hillel and Shammai as the one that does.

review.q: Which statement follows the course's rule for describing how groups read the Akhnai story?
choices: Reform readers are the only ones who understand it
Orthodox readers are wrong about it
The story proves the law changes
Each group draws its own lesson, and the text does not settle which is right
review.why: The course describes how Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers read the text without ranking them.
